title: Reading: skim before scanning
body: Original lesson: First skim the passage for its topic, paragraph purpose and structure. Then read the question carefully and identify key words. Scan for the idea, not just an identical word: IELTS passages often paraphrase. Read the sentence before and after the match to confirm meaning. Do not answer from outside knowledge.

title: Reading: True / False / Not Given
body: Original lesson: TRUE means the passage agrees with the statement. FALSE means the passage directly contradicts it. NOT GIVEN means the passage does not provide enough information to decide. Do not treat a statement as FALSE simply because the passage does not mention it. Underline the exact evidence before choosing.

title: Reading: matching headings
body: Original lesson: Read the first and last sentences, then identify the paragraph's central purpose. A heading should summarise the whole paragraph rather than one example. Cross out headings that are too narrow, too broad or focus on a detail that appears only once.

title: Reading: manage the 60-minute test
body: Original lesson: Practise allocating time across three passages. If a question is taking too long, mark it and move on. Transfer answers carefully and check word limits for completion tasks. Build accuracy first, then increase speed. Track whether errors come from vocabulary, locating evidence or misreading instructions.

title: Reading: completion questions
body: Original lesson: Check the instruction for the maximum number of words. Predict the grammar of the missing item (noun, verb, number or adjective). Use the passage's wording unless the task says otherwise. After filling the blank, read the complete sentence to check grammar and meaning.

title: Listening: predict the answer type
body: Original lesson: Before audio begins, inspect the questions and predict whether each answer should be a date, name, number, place or noun. Listen for meaning and paraphrase rather than waiting for exact wording. Keep moving if you miss one answer; the next item may begin quickly.

title: Listening: numbers, dates and spelling
body: Original lesson: Practise distinguishing similar numbers, letter names and dates. Listen for corrections such as 'Tuesday—sorry, Thursday'. Check plural endings, spelling and units. Follow the stated word limit and do not add extra words that make an otherwise correct answer invalid.

title: Listening: maps and directions
body: Original lesson: Read the map labels before listening. Identify the starting point and orientation. Listen for relational language such as opposite, beyond, next to, at the end of and on the left. Trace the route as you hear it instead of trying to remember the entire description afterwards.

title: Listening: review errors by category
body: Original lesson: After practice, classify each mistake: missed a keyword, misunderstood paraphrase, lost place, spelling error, number confusion or word-limit error. Replay only where legally permitted and compare your notes. A category-based error log makes the next practice session more targeted.

title: Listening: note completion
body: Original lesson: Use the context around a gap to predict grammar and topic. Write a short answer while listening and check it against the sentence afterwards. Do not wait for the end of the recording to fill every blank, because details may not be repeated.

title: Writing Task 2: unpack the prompt
body: Original lesson: Identify the topic, task instruction and every part of the question. 'Discuss both views and give your opinion' requires both views plus your position. 'To what extent' requires a clear degree of agreement. Plan a direct answer before writing; do not memorise an essay unrelated to the exact prompt.

title: Writing Task 2: build a paragraph
body: Original lesson: A strong body paragraph usually contains one main claim, an explanation of why it matters, and a relevant example or consequence. Keep each paragraph focused. Examples should support the argument rather than introduce a new, unrelated point.

title: Writing Task 2: cohesion without over-linking
body: Original lesson: Use pronouns, logical sequencing and repeated key concepts to connect ideas. Linking expressions should clarify the relationship between sentences, not decorate every sentence. Too many formulaic phrases can make writing mechanical. Read the paragraph aloud to check whether the logic is clear without the connectors.

title: Writing Task 1 Academic: overview first
body: Original lesson: In chart or graph tasks, identify the largest overall trends, highest and lowest values, and major contrasts. Include an overview without listing every number. Group comparable data and report figures accurately. Do not explain why a trend occurred unless the visual provides that information.

title: Writing: edit in two passes
body: Original lesson: First check task response, organisation and whether every part of the prompt is answered. Then check sentence-level issues: subject–verb agreement, articles, verb tense, countable nouns, punctuation and spelling. Editing every sentence while drafting can interrupt the argument; reserve time for a final review.

title: Writing: academic vocabulary precision
body: Original lesson: Prefer accurate words to rare words used incorrectly. Avoid memorised phrases that do not fit the topic. Check collocations, word forms and whether a word expresses the intended strength. Use a range of structures naturally, and prioritise clear meaning over complexity for its own sake.

title: Speaking Part 1: extend naturally
body: Original lesson: Answer the question directly, then add a reason, detail or brief example. Two to four sentences are often enough. Avoid one-word replies, but do not turn simple questions into memorised speeches. Focus on natural rhythm and accurate everyday language.

title: Speaking Part 2: use notes, not a script
body: Original lesson: Use the preparation minute to note keywords under the cue-card prompts. Organise the answer in a simple sequence such as background, event or detail, and reflection. Notes should remind you of ideas, not contain complete sentences to read aloud.

title: Speaking Part 3: develop an argument
body: Original lesson: Part 3 questions often ask for comparison, causes, effects or predictions. State your view, explain the reasoning and illustrate it with an example. You can qualify a claim using 'in some cases' or 'this depends on'. Avoid unsupported absolute statements.

title: Speaking: fluency and repair
body: Original lesson: Fluency does not mean speaking without any pause. Use brief planning pauses and repair a sentence calmly if you make a mistake. Avoid repeatedly restarting the entire answer. Record short responses and notice long pauses, repeated words and whether ideas connect logically.

title: Speaking: pronunciation practice
body: Original lesson: Prioritise intelligibility, word stress, sentence stress and meaningful chunking. Practise shadowing short, lawful audio clips and record yourself. You do not need to imitate a particular accent. Review whether key words are clear and whether intonation helps the listener follow your meaning.

title: Speaking: build a topic vocabulary notebook
body: Original lesson: Record useful phrases in context rather than memorising long lists. For each topic, save collocations, a personal example and one alternative way to express an idea. Revisit the phrases in new answers so you can use them flexibly rather than forcing them into every response.

title: IELTS study plan: 30-minute daily routine
body: Original lesson: A balanced 30-minute session can include 5 minutes reviewing previous errors, 15 minutes on one targeted skill, 5 minutes checking answers against evidence or criteria, and 5 minutes recording the next action. Rotate skills across the week and include timed practice as test day approaches.

title: IELTS band scores: interpret feedback carefully
body: Original lesson: Automated feedback can help you identify patterns but it is not an official IELTS score. Use the official public band descriptors and guidance when reviewing performance. Track repeated strengths and weaknesses over multiple tasks rather than making a decision from a single short exercise.
